title: Chapter III
paragraphs: As she led me upstairs, she advised me to hide the candle and make no noise. Her master had a strange feeling about the bedroom she was taking me to, and never willingly allowed anyone to sleep there. I asked why. She did not know, she said: she had lived there only a year or two, and so many odd things went on that she could not begin to wonder about them.

Too dazed to feel curious myself, I secured the door and looked round for the bed. The entire furniture was a chair, a wardrobe and a large oak box, with square openings near its top like the windows of a coach. I went over and looked inside. It proved to be a peculiar old-fashioned bed, cleverly designed to save every member of the family from needing a separate room. In effect it made a little enclosed chamber, and the sill of a window contained within it served as a table.
I slid the panelled sides back, climbed in with my candle, and closed them again, feeling safe from Heathcliff's watchfulness and everyone else's.

The window ledge where I set my candle had a few mouldy books stacked in one corner, and its paint was covered with scratched writing. The writing consisted only of a name, repeated in every sort of lettering, large and small: _Catherine Earnshaw_, changed here and there to _Catherine Heathcliff_, and then to _Catherine Linton_.

With dull indifference I rested my head against the window and went on spelling out Catherine Earnshaw—Heathcliff—Linton until my eyes shut. They had been closed less than five minutes when blazing white letters sprang out of the dark, as vivid as ghosts: the air swarmed with Catherines. Rousing myself to drive away the intrusive name, I discovered that the wick of my candle had bent over onto one of the old books, filling the place with the scent of scorched calfskin.

I trimmed it off and, feeling thoroughly uncomfortable with cold and the remains of my nausea, sat up and opened the damaged volume across my knees. It was a Testament in thin print, with an awful musty smell. A blank leaf carried the inscription “Catherine Earnshaw, her book,” and a date about twenty-five years earlier.

I closed it and picked up another, then another, until I had inspected them all. Catherine's library was small and select, and the books' battered condition showed they had been well used, though not entirely for their proper purpose. Scarcely a chapter had escaped a pen-and-ink commentary—or what looked like one—filling every scrap of space the printer had left blank. Some passages were disconnected sentences; others made a regular diary, scrawled in an unformed child's handwriting. At the head of an extra page, probably a great treasure when first discovered, I was delighted to find an excellent caricature of my friend Joseph, roughly but forcefully drawn. I immediately felt interested in this unknown Catherine and began at once to make out her faded hieroglyphics.

“A dreadful Sunday,” began the paragraph below. “I wish my father would come back. Hindley is a hateful replacement—he treats Heathcliff horribly—H. and I mean to rebel—we made our first move this evening.

“Rain poured down all day, so we couldn't go to church. Joseph therefore had to organise a congregation in the attic, while Hindley and his wife lounged downstairs by a comfortable fire—doing anything but reading their Bibles, I'll swear. Heathcliff, the miserable ploughboy and I were ordered to take our prayer books and go up. There we sat in a row on a sack of grain, groaning and shivering, and hoping Joseph would shiver too, so he'd shorten the sermon for his own comfort. A useless hope! The service lasted exactly three hours, yet my brother had the nerve to exclaim as we came down, ‘What, finished already?’ We used to be allowed to play on Sunday evenings if we kept reasonably quiet; now the slightest giggle gets us sent into corners.

“‘You forget there's a master here,’ says the tyrant. ‘I'll destroy the first of you who makes me lose my temper! I demand absolute seriousness and silence. Ah, boy! Was that you? Frances, darling, pull his hair as you pass: I heard him snap his fingers.’ Frances pulled his hair with enthusiasm, then sat on her husband's knee, and there they stayed like a pair of babies, kissing and talking nonsense for hours—silly chatter we would have been ashamed of. We made ourselves as comfortable as we could in the arch under the dresser. I had just fastened our pinafores together and hung them up as a curtain when Joseph came in on an errand from the stables. He tears down my work, boxes my ears and croaks:

“‘T' master's nobbut just buried, and t' Sabbath isn't over, and t' sound o' t' gospel's still in yer ears, and ye dare go playing! Shame on ye! Sit ye down, wicked children! There's good books enough, if ye'll read 'em: sit down and think about yer souls!’

“With these words he forced us to arrange ourselves where a dull ray from the distant fire would let us read the rubbish he thrust on us. I could not stand the task. I grabbed my grimy volume by the spine and hurled it into the dog kennel, declaring I hated a good book. Heathcliff kicked his into the same place. Then there was an uproar!

“‘Master Hindley!’ our chaplain shouted. ‘Master, come here! Miss Cathy's torn t' back off “The Helmet o' Salvation,” and Heathcliff's kicked his foot into t' first part o' “The Broad Way to Destruction!” It's fair frightening ye let 'em carry on this way. Eh! T' old man would ha' thrashed 'em properly—but he's gone!’

“Hindley hurried from his paradise beside the fire, grabbed one of us by the collar and the other by the arm, and threw us both into the back kitchen. There, Joseph assured us, ‘old Nick’ would come for us as surely as we were alive. Comforted in this fashion, we each found a separate corner to await his arrival. I got this book and a pot of ink from a shelf and pushed the house door ajar for light. Writing has passed twenty minutes for me, but my companion is impatient. He suggests we take the dairymaid's cloak and run out over the moors under its shelter. A pleasant idea—and if the surly old man comes in, he can think his prophecy has come true. We can't get any wetter or colder in the rain than we are here.”
I suppose Catherine carried out her plan, because the next sentence turned to a different subject: she became tearful.

“I never imagined Hindley could make me cry so much!” she wrote. “My head aches until I can't bear it on the pillow, and still I can't stop. Poor Heathcliff! Hindley calls him a vagabond and won't let him sit or eat with us any more. He says we mustn't play together, and threatens to throw him out of the house if we disobey. He's been blaming our father—how dare he?—for treating H. too generously, and swears he'll put him back where he belongs—”

I began to nod over the faint writing, my eyes straying from the handwriting to the print. I saw a red, decorated title: “Seventy Times Seven, and the First of the Seventy-First. A Pious Discourse delivered by the Reverend Jabez Branderham, in the Chapel of Gimmerden Sough.” While I was still half-consciously puzzling over what Jabez Branderham would make of his subject, I sank back into bed and fell asleep. Alas, what bad tea and bad temper can do! What else could have given me such a dreadful night? I cannot remember another to compare with it in all the time I have been capable of suffering.

I started dreaming almost before I stopped knowing where I was. I thought it was morning and I had set out for home with Joseph as my guide. Snow lay yards deep along our road; as we struggled through it, my companion exhausted me with constant complaints that I had brought no pilgrim's staff. He said I could never get into the house without one, and proudly waved a heavy-headed club, which I understood was what he meant by that name. For a moment I thought it absurd to need such a weapon to enter my own home. Then a fresh idea struck me. We were not going there: we were on our way to hear the famous Jabez Branderham preach on the text “Seventy Times Seven.” Either Joseph, the preacher or I had committed the “First of the Seventy-First,” and was to be publicly exposed and cast out of the church.

We reached the chapel. I have actually passed it two or three times on my walks. It stands in a hollow between two hills—a high hollow near a marsh, whose peaty damp is said to preserve the few bodies buried there as well as embalming would. The roof has remained intact so far; but the minister's pay is only twenty pounds a year and a two-roomed house threatening shortly to collapse into one room, so no clergyman will take on the parish. This is particularly understandable given the common report that his flock would prefer to let him starve rather than add a penny from their own pockets to his income. In my dream, however, Jabez had a full and attentive congregation; and he preached—good God, what a sermon! It was divided into _four hundred and ninety_ parts, each as long as an ordinary sermon, and each dealing with a separate sin! Where he found them all I cannot say. He interpreted the phrase in his own way, and apparently the brother had to commit a different sin on every occasion. They were the strangest offences: peculiar transgressions I had never even imagined.

Oh, how tired I became. How I squirmed and yawned, nodded and woke again! How I pinched and pricked myself, rubbed my eyes, stood up, sat down, and nudged Joseph to ask whether the man would _ever_ finish. I was sentenced to hear it all. At last he reached the “_First of the Seventy-First_.” At this crisis a sudden inspiration came upon me: I felt called to rise and denounce Jabez Branderham as the sinner whose sin no Christian was obliged to forgive.

“Sir,” I cried, “sitting in these four walls without a break, I have endured and forgiven the four hundred and ninety divisions of your sermon. Seventy times seven times I have picked up my hat and prepared to leave—seventy times seven times you have absurdly forced me back into my seat. The four hundred and ninety-first is beyond endurance. Fellow sufferers, attack him! Pull him down and crush him to atoms, so that the place which knows him may know him no more!”

“_Thou art the Man!_” cried Jabez after a solemn pause, leaning over his cushion. “Seventy times seven times you twisted your face in yawns—seventy times seven I consulted my soul: behold, this is human weakness; this too may be forgiven! The First of the Seventy-First has arrived. Brothers, carry out the judgment written against him. Such honour have all His saints!”

At that last word the entire gathering raised their pilgrim's staffs and rushed together upon me. With no weapon to lift in my defence, I began wrestling for Joseph's, since he was my nearest and fiercest attacker. As the crowd surged together, several clubs crossed and blows meant for me struck other heads. Soon the whole chapel rang with blows and answering blows: every man's hand was against his neighbour. Branderham, unwilling to stand idle, poured out his zeal by hammering loudly on the wooden pulpit. Its boards answered so sharply that at last, to my inexpressible relief, they woke me. And what had suggested this tremendous uproar? What had played Jabez's part in the commotion? Only a fir branch touching my window as the wind howled past, rattling its dry cones against the panes! I listened uncertainly for a moment, identified the troublemaker, then turned over, dozed and dreamed again—if possible, more unpleasantly than before.

This time I remembered I was lying in the oak enclosure, and clearly heard the gusting wind and the driving snow. I also heard the fir branch repeating its irritating noise, and correctly recognised its cause; but it bothered me so much that I decided to silence it if I could. I thought I got up and tried to undo the window catch. The hook was soldered into its fastening, something I had noticed while awake but forgotten. “I must stop it all the same!” I muttered, driving my knuckles through the glass and reaching out to catch the troublesome branch. Instead my fingers closed around the fingers of a small, ice-cold hand!
The overwhelming horror of a nightmare seized me. I tried to pull my arm back, but the hand held on, and a voice full of misery sobbed,
“Let me in—let me in!”
“Who are you?” I demanded, struggling all the while to free myself.
“Catherine Linton,” came the shivering answer—why did I think of _Linton_? I had read _Earnshaw_ twenty times for every Linton—“I've come home: I lost my way on the moor!”

As it spoke, I dimly made out a child's face peering through the window. Fear made me cruel. Finding I could not shake the creature off, I dragged its wrist onto the broken glass and rubbed it backwards and forwards until blood ran down and soaked the bedclothes. Still it wailed, “Let me in!” and kept its stubborn grip, almost driving me mad with terror.
“How can I!” I said at last. “Let _me_ go, then, if you want me to let you inside!”
The fingers loosened. I jerked my hand back through the hole, quickly piled the books in a pyramid against it, and blocked my ears against the pitiful pleading.
I seemed to hold them shut for more than fifteen minutes; but the moment I listened again, that sorrowful cry was still moaning on!
“Go away!” I shouted. “I won't ever let you in, even if you beg for twenty years.”
“It has been twenty years,” the voice mourned. “Twenty years. I've wandered homeless for twenty years!”
Then a faint scratching began outside, and the pile of books shifted as though something were pushing it forward.
I tried to leap up but could not move a limb, and screamed aloud in a frenzy of terror.

To my embarrassment, I discovered that the scream was no dream. Quick footsteps came towards my bedroom; someone pushed the door open forcefully, and light shone through the square openings at the top of the bed. I was still sitting there shivering and wiping sweat from my forehead. The intruder seemed to hesitate, muttering to himself.
Finally he spoke in something near a whisper, clearly expecting no reply:
“Is somebody in here?”
I thought it best to admit I was there, recognising Heathcliff's voice and fearing he would search further if I stayed silent.
Accordingly I turned and slid the panels open. I will not readily forget the effect of that movement.

Heathcliff stood near the doorway in his shirt and trousers, candle wax dripping over his fingers, his face as white as the wall behind him. The first creak of the oak struck him like an electric shock. The candle flew several feet out of his hand, and he was so violently shaken that he could scarcely pick it up.

“It's only your guest, sir,” I called, wishing to spare him the humiliation of displaying more of his fear. “Unfortunately a dreadful nightmare made me scream in my sleep. I'm sorry to have disturbed you.”

“Oh, God damn you, Mr. Lockwood! I wish you were at the—” my host began, putting the candle on a chair because he could not hold it still. “And who brought you up to this room?” he went on, digging his nails into his palms and grinding his teeth to control his trembling jaws. “Who was it? I've a good mind to throw them out of the house this instant!”

“Your servant Zillah,” I answered, jumping onto the floor and hurriedly getting dressed. “I wouldn't object if you did, Mr. Heathcliff; she thoroughly deserves it. I suppose she wanted further proof that the room was haunted, at my expense. Well, it is—it's crawling with ghosts and goblins! You're quite right to keep it locked up, I assure you. Nobody will thank you for a nap in a den like this!”

“What are you talking about?” Heathcliff asked. “And what are you doing? Lie down and spend the rest of the night here, since you _are_ here; but for Heaven's sake! Don't make that horrible noise again: nothing could justify it unless someone was cutting your throat!”

“If that little devil had come through the window, she'd probably have strangled me!” I retorted. “I won't put up with your hospitable ancestors tormenting me again. Wasn't the Reverend Jabez Branderham a relation on your mother's side? And that minx, Catherine Linton or Earnshaw, or whatever her name was—she must have been a changeling—wicked little soul! She told me she'd wandered the earth for twenty years: a deserved punishment for her sins in life, I've no doubt!”

Almost as soon as I had spoken, I remembered how Heathcliff's name was joined to Catherine's in the book. That fact had entirely escaped my memory until my words recalled it. I blushed at my thoughtlessness, but hurried to add, without otherwise acknowledging my offence, “The truth is, sir, I spent the first part of the night—” Here I stopped again. I had been about to say “reading those old books,” which would have revealed my knowledge of their handwritten contents as well as the print. I corrected myself and continued: “spelling out the name scratched on that window ledge. A monotonous pastime, likely to send me to sleep, like counting, or—”

“What _can_ you mean, speaking like this to _me!_” Heathcliff thundered with savage force. “How—how _dare_ you, beneath my own roof?—God! He must be mad to speak so!” And he struck his forehead in fury.

I could not decide whether to take offence or continue explaining; but he seemed so deeply affected that I pitied him and went on describing my dreams. I insisted I had never heard the name “Catherine Linton” before; reading it repeatedly had merely left an impression which took human form when I no longer controlled my imagination. While I spoke, Heathcliff gradually retreated behind the bed, finally sitting down almost hidden by it. From his uneven, broken breathing, however, I guessed he was struggling to master a surge of violent feeling. Unwilling to show that I had heard this struggle, I noisily continued dressing, consulted my watch and talked to myself about the length of the night. “Not three yet! I could have sworn it was six. Time stands still here: surely we must have gone to bed at eight!”

“Always nine in winter, and up at four,” my host answered, stifling a groan and, if I read the shadow of his moving arm correctly, brushing a tear from his eyes. “Mr. Lockwood,” he added, “you can use my room. You'll only be in the way if you go downstairs so early, and that childish screaming has sent all chance of sleep to the devil for me.”

“And for me,” I replied. “I'll walk round the yard until daylight, then leave. You needn't fear another intrusion. I'm thoroughly cured now of looking for pleasure in company, whether in the country or the town. A sensible man ought to find enough companionship in himself.”

“Charming company!” Heathcliff muttered. “Take the candle and go wherever you want. I'll join you shortly. Keep out of the yard, though: the dogs are loose; and in the sitting room—Juno stands guard there, and—no, you can only wander along the passages and stairs. But go on! I'll come in two minutes!”

I obeyed far enough to leave the room, but, not knowing where the narrow passages led, I stood still. Thus I unwillingly witnessed an act of superstition from my landlord oddly at variance with his apparent good sense. He climbed onto the bed and wrenched open the window, breaking into an uncontrollable storm of tears as he pulled at it. “Come in! Come in!” he sobbed. “Cathy, please come. Oh, do—_once_ more! Oh! My heart's darling! Hear me _this_ time, Catherine, at last!” The ghost displayed the usual wilfulness of ghosts: it gave no sign of existing. But wind and snow whirled wildly inside, reaching even where I stood and blowing out the candle.

The flood of grief accompanying his ravings held such anguish that pity made me forget their foolishness. I withdrew, half angry at having heard anything, and upset that I had told him my ridiculous nightmare and caused such agony—although _why_ it had done so was beyond me. I cautiously made my way downstairs and arrived in the back kitchen, where a little glow from the fire, raked together into a compact heap, allowed me to relight my candle. Nothing moved except a grey tabby cat, which crept out of the ashes and greeted me with a complaining mew.

Two curved benches almost enclosed the hearth. I stretched out on one, and Grimalkin climbed onto the other. We were both nodding before anyone disturbed our retreat. It was Joseph, shuffling down a wooden ladder that disappeared through a hatch in the roof—the way to his attic, I suppose. He gave a dark look at the small flame I had coaxed up between the bars, swept the cat from its perch, and sat in its place to begin packing tobacco into a three-inch pipe. My presence in his sanctuary was evidently an impertinence too disgraceful for words: he silently put the pipe between his lips, folded his arms and puffed away. I let him enjoy this luxury undisturbed; and after drawing out the final curl of smoke and giving a deep sigh, he rose and left as solemnly as he had arrived.

Next came a livelier footstep. I opened my mouth to say good morning but shut it again before delivering the greeting, for Hareton Earnshaw was saying his prayers _sotto voce_ in a succession of curses against everything he touched. He was rummaging in a corner for a spade or shovel to dig through the snowdrifts. He glanced over the back of the bench, nostrils flaring, and no more considered exchanging courtesies with me than with my companion the cat. His preparations suggested to me that going outside was permitted; I left my hard bed and moved to follow. Seeing this, he pushed at an inner door with the end of his spade and made an inarticulate noise to indicate that this was where I must go if I wanted a change of place.

The door opened into the sitting room, where the women were already at work: Zillah driving tongues of flame up the chimney with an enormous pair of bellows, and Mrs. Heathcliff kneeling on the hearth, reading by the blaze. She held a hand between her eyes and the furnace heat and seemed entirely absorbed in her book. She paused only to scold the servant for showering her with sparks, or occasionally to push away a dog thrusting its nosing muzzle too boldly into her face. I was surprised to find Heathcliff there too. He stood facing the fire, his back to me, just finishing a furious scene with poor Zillah. Every now and then she stopped working to lift a corner of her apron and let out an indignant groan.

“And you, you worthless—” he burst out as I entered, turning to his daughter-in-law and using an animal name as harmless as duck or sheep, though usually printed as a dash—. “There you are, up to your idle tricks again! The others earn their food—you live on my charity! Put that rubbish away and find yourself some work. You'll pay me for the torment of having you always before my eyes—do you hear, you damned hussy?”

“I'll put my rubbish away because you can force me if I don't,” the young woman answered, shutting her book and throwing it onto a chair. “But even if you swear your tongue out, I won't do anything except what I choose!”

Heathcliff raised a hand, and she sprang out of reach, evidently familiar with its weight. Having no desire to watch a cat-and-dog fight, I stepped briskly forward as though eager for the warmth of the fire and entirely unaware of the quarrel I had interrupted. Both had enough manners to stop fighting. Heathcliff put his fists in his pockets, away from temptation; Mrs. Heathcliff curled her lip and went to a distant chair, where she kept her promise by acting the statue for the rest of my visit. That was brief. I refused breakfast and at the first hint of dawn seized a chance to escape into the open air, now clear, still and as cold as invisible ice.

Before I reached the far end of the garden my landlord called for me to stop and offered to guide me over the moor. It was fortunate he did: the whole hillside was a rolling white ocean, its rises and hollows giving no reliable sign of the ground beneath. Many pits, at least, had been filled level, and entire ridges of quarry waste had vanished from the map left in my mind by yesterday's walk. I had noticed a line of upright stones beside the road, six or seven yards apart, running the whole length of the waste. These had been set up and coated with lime expressly to guide travellers in darkness, and when snow like this blurred the distinction between the firm path and the deep bogs on either side. Now, apart from a dirty point sticking up here and there, every trace of them had disappeared. My companion often had to tell me to bear right or left when I thought I was faithfully following the road's curves.

We spoke very little. At the entrance to Thrushcross Park he stopped, saying I could not go wrong from there. A hurried bow served for our farewells, and I pressed on using my own judgment, for the gatekeeper's lodge is still empty. It is two miles from the gate to the Grange; I believe I made it four by losing my way among the trees and sinking into snow up to my neck—a situation only those who have experienced it can appreciate. Whatever route I took, the clock was striking twelve when I entered the house: exactly one hour for every mile of the usual journey from Wuthering Heights.

My human fixture and her satellites rushed to greet me, exclaiming all at once that they had entirely given me up. Everyone had assumed I had died during the night, and they were wondering how to begin searching for my remains. I told them to be quiet now they could see I had returned, and dragged myself upstairs, numb to the heart. After changing into dry clothes and pacing up and down for thirty or forty minutes to restore my body's warmth, I retired to my study as weak as a kitten—almost too weak to enjoy the cheerful fire and steaming coffee the servant had prepared to revive me.
